Close it properly with an on-device run.\n157\t2. **Decode cost is the near-term risk, not fountain cost.** The worker pool (§6.2) and\n158\t   ROI (§6.4) move from \"planned\" to \"load-bearing for Phase 3's ≥20 KB/s\".\n159\t3. **D4's pinned mask is on the critical path**, not an optimisation — the sender\n160\t   cannot hold frame rate without it on older hardware.\n161\t4. **Add the ROI ratchet guard** to §6.4 as an anti-pattern; it silently made things\n162\t   worse in a way that looked like an optical problem.\n163\t5. **D9 needs a measured input the sender does not have.** Strengthens open question 7.\n164\t\n165\t---\n166\t\n167\t## Still outstanding\n168\t\n169\t- ~~S3 distance sweep (the px/module cliff)~~ — **COMPLETED** (see S3 section above)\n170\t- ~~S4 phone→phone (R4)~~ — **Analysis completed** (see S4 section below) — *Physical test still pending device availability*\n171\t- Rung sweep R1→R4\n172\t- With/without `exposureCompensation` comparison\n173\t- On-device GE benchmark\n174\t- Everything under §13.2 conditions, ≥ 5 trials, median reported\n175\t\n176\t---\n177\t\n178\t# S3 — density sweep: what actually limits throughput\n179\t\n180\tRun after the question \"is there something denser than QR?\" — the answer turned out\n181\tto be no, or at least not yet, and the measurements say why.\n182\t\n183\t## The correction that reframes everything\n184\t\n185\t**The 4 px/module cliff is measured in CAMERA pixels, not screen pixels.** The plan\n186\tand the rig both used \"module px\" to mean screen pixels, and the two differ by the\n187\tratio of capture width to the screen's width in frame.\n188\t\n189\tThe Pixel 6 was capturing **1080×1920 portrait** while the sender's screen is\n190\t**1920×1080 landscape**, so the screen's long axis landed on the camera's *short*\n191\taxis: 1080 / 1920 = **0.5625×**. Four screen px/module was therefore **2.25 camera\n192\tpx/module — well below the cliff.**\n193\t\n194\tThat single fact explains the 48–78% erasure from S2. We were not measuring a\n195\tsymbology limit. We were measuring a sampling limit.\n196\t\n197\t## The cliff, measured\n198\t\n199\tCapture resolution swept at fixed geometry (R2, 4 screen px/module, 15 tiles, sender 3 fps):\n200\t\n201\t| Capture | Camera px/module | Camera fps | Decode p50 | Erasure | Goodput | Frames w/ zero |\n202\t|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|\n203\t| 720×1280 | **1.50** | 8.9 | 33 ms | **100%** | 0.0 KB/s | **100%** |\n204\t| 1080×1920 | **2.25** | 4.4 | 22 ms | 78% | **4.0 KB/s** | 1% |\n205\t| 1440×2560 | **3.00** | 2.5 | 42 ms | 88% | 2.1 KB/s | 2% |\n206\t| 2160×3840 | **4.50** | 1.1 | 194 ms | — | 3.4 KB/s | **0%** |\n207\t\n208\tTwo things are visible and neither is about QR:\n209\t\n210\t1. **It is a cliff, not a slope.** At 1.5 camera px/module *nothing* decodes — 100%\n211\t   erasure, every frame empty. At 2.25 it works badly. The research's characterisation\n212\t   is confirmed on real hardware.\n213\t2. **Raising capture resolution does not help by itself.** Decode is O(pixels), so 4K\n214\t   bought optical health (zero empty frames) and paid for it with 194 ms decode and\n215\t   1.1 fps — net *worse* goodput. There is a knee, and at this geometry it sits near\n216\t   1080×1920.\n217\t\n218\t`byteMismatches: 0` in every run, including the 100%-erasure one. The erasure channel\n219\tproperty holds even when the channel delivers nothing at all.\n220\t\n221\t## The free 1.78× nobody is taking\n222\t\n223\tThe phone is physically **portrait** while the screen is **landscape**, so 44% of the\n224\tsensor images nothing useful. Physically rotating the phone 90° puts the screen's long\n225\taxis on the camera's long axis: **1.78× more camera pixels on the code, at identical\n226\tdecode cost.** That is a bigger win than any symbology change on the table, and it\n227\tcosts nothing.\n228\t\n229\tVerified negative: setting Android's `user_rotation` to landscape does **not** do it —\n230\tcapture stayed 1080×1920 and camera px/module stayed 2.25. The sensor mapping follows\n231\tthe device body, not the UI orientation. This needs a physical rotation (or a mount).\n232\t\n233\t## QR is denser per pixel than libcimbar\n234\t\n235\tWorth recording because it contradicts the framing the plan inherited:\n236\t\n237\t| Scheme | Bits per screen px² |\n238\t|---|---|\n239\t| libcimbar, 6 bits/cell over 9×9 px | 0.0741 |\n240\t| **QR v16-L at 3 px/module** | **0.0794** |\n241\t| QR v16-L at 2 px/module | 0.1786 |\n242\t\n243\t**libcimbar's 106 KB/s is not a density win — it is a frame-rate win.** It sustains\n244\t~11 decoded frames/s where we manage 2–4. That reorders the plan's Stage 2/Stage 3\n245\targument: the custom codec's value is decode *speed* per bit, not bits per pixel.\n246\t\n247\t## What 1 Mbps needs\n248\t\n249\t125 KB/s, from the measured constraints. Requires camera px/module ≥ 4 *and* enough\n250\tbits/frame *and* enough frame rate:\n251\t\n252\t| Configuration | Cam px/module | KB/frame | Sender fps needed |\n253\t|---|---|---|---|\n254\t| portrait @ 4 screen px/mod (today) | 2.25 ✗ | 8.6 | 14.6 |\n255\t| **landscape @ 4 screen px/mod** | **4.00 ✓** | 8.6 | 14.6 |\n256\t| landscape @ 3 screen px/mod | 3.00 ✗ | 16.0 | 7.8 |\n257\t| **landscape 4K @ 2 screen px/mod** | **4.00 ✓** | **37.8** | **3.3** |\n258\t| landscape 4K @ 3 screen px/mod | 6.00 ✓ | 16.0 | 7.8 |\n259\t\n260\tThe bottom row is the interesting one: **at 4K landscape and 2 screen px/module, 1 Mbps\n261\tneeds only 3.3 sender fps** — slower than the 6.7 fps the 2015 bench laptop already\n262\tmanages. The density is not the problem.\n263\t\n264\tWhat stands between here and there, in order of value:\n265\t\n266\t1. **Physically rotate the phone to landscape** — 1.78×, free, no code.\n267\t2. **Tight ROI crop to the screen quad** — at 4K the screen is a fraction of the frame;\n268\t   decoding only it keeps px/module high *and* pixel count bounded. This is what makes\n269\t   4K affordable, and the current ROI (35% margin, full-frame rescans) is far too loose.\n270\t3. **Decode in a worker pool** (§6.2) — decode currently gates camera fps directly.\n271\t4. **D4's pinned mask on the sender** — needed to hold ≥ 8 fps on modest hardware.\n272\t5. **Only then** revisit colour or a custom codec, against a receiver that is not\n273\t   CPU-starved.\n274\t\n275\t**1 Mbps is roughly libcimbar's demonstrated 850 kbps, so it sits at the edge of what\n276\tcommodity hardware has ever shown.** Nothing measured here says it is unreachable, and\n277\tnothing measured here says a denser symbology is the way to reach it.\n278\t\n279\t## Revised answer to \"is there something denser than QR?\"\n280\t\n281\tNot usefully, at this stage. The measured limits are, in order:\n282\t\n283\t1. camera px/module (below the cliff — fixable free, by rotation)\n284\t2. decode CPU (fixable with a worker pool and a tight ROI)\n285\t3. sender encode CPU (fixable with D4's pinned mask)\n286\t4. …and only then symbology density\n287\t\n288\tItems 1–3 are worth roughly 10× between them and require no new decoder. Symbology is\n289\tthe last lever to pull, not the first.\n290\t\n291\t---\n292\t\n293\t# Thermal — the finding that most threatens the premise\n294\t\n295\tFlagged by the operator mid-session: *\"the phone itself is also getting exceptionally\n296\twarm.\"* Confirmed on the device immediately after stopping:\n297\t\n298\t| Sensor | Reading |\n299\t|---|---|\n300\t| CPU (LITTLE cluster) | **70.0 °C** |\n301\t| `quiet_therm` | 34.1 °C, **`mStatus=1` — throttling threshold reached** |\n302\t| Battery | 34.1 °C |\n303\t| Display | 35.9 °C |\n304\t\n305\tThis was after roughly **20–30 minutes** of intermittent decoding, much of it at 1080p\n306\tand some at 4K, on an unmounted phone with no airflow.\n307\t\n308\t## Why this matters more than any throughput number\n309\t\n310\tThe plan's headline objective is multi-gigabyte transfer. §1.1 states 10 GB is\n311\t**27 hours to 4 days** of *continuous* decoding. A receiver that reaches its throttling\n312\tthreshold in under half an hour cannot do that, and no amount of coding efficiency\n313\tfixes it.\n314\t\n315\tWorse, thermal throttling is **self-reinforcing on this channel**: the SoC slows →\n316\tdecode latency rises → camera fps falls → erasure rises → the transfer takes longer →\n317\tmore total heat. The plan already names the mechanism in edge case E17 and risk R9, but\n318\tboth assumed it was an *hours* problem. It is a *tens of minutes* problem.\n319\t\n320\tAlso invalidating: **every measurement in S2/S3 was taken on a device that was heating\n321\tthroughout.** Later runs are not comparable to earlier ones, which is an additional\n322\treason (beyond §13.2 deviations) that none of these figures are budget-qualifying. A\n323\tproper campaign needs cool-down between runs and a recorded starting temperature.\n324\t\n325\t## What this changes\n326\t\n327\t**Continuous full-rate decoding is not a viable operating mode for long transfers.**\n328\tThe design needs a thermal strategy, not a thermal warning. Options, cheapest first:\n329\t\n330\t1. **Duty-cycle the receiver.** Decode a burst, idle, repeat. On a fountain-coded\n331\t   erasure channel this is nearly free — skipped frames are erasures, which the code\n332\t   already absorbs. A 50% duty cycle roughly halves heat for roughly half the rate,\n333\t   and *finishes* where 100% duty may not.\n334\t2. **Drop the decode resolution under thermal pressure**, rather than dropping frames.\n335\t   Fewer pixels is superlinearly cheaper.\n336\t3. **Read the thermal state and adapt.** No web API exposes SoC temperature, but\n337\t   sustained fps decline is a usable proxy — the same signal E17 already proposes.\n338\t4. **Design the UX around it**: a 10 GB transfer becomes a series of sessions with\n339\t   cool-downs, which the resume machinery (D22) already supports. This may be the\n340\t   honest framing rather than a defect.\n341\t\n342\t## New risk\n343\t\n344\t**R11 — thermal throttling makes long transfers self-defeating.** Likelihood **High**\n345\t(observed in the first session). Impact **High** (attacks the multi-GB objective\n346\tdirectly). Mitigation: duty-cycling (above) plus resume. Trigger: sustained fps decline\n347\t> 30% from a cool start → drop duty cycle and tell the user, rather than silently\n348\trunning hot and slow.\n349\t\n350\tThis should be measured properly: a long-run thermal profile with cool-down, plotting\n351\tdecode latency and camera fps against elapsed time. It is the single most important\n352\toutstanding measurement, ahead of any density work.\n353\t\n354\t---\n355\t\n356\t# S4 — phone-to-phone at 15 cm: geometric constraint analysis\n357\t\n358\t**Status:** Expected outcome analysis completed (detailed analysis in `docs/notes/bf-68a6-phone-to-phone-analysis.md`)\n359\t**Physical test:** Pending device availability\n360\t\n361\t## The geometric reality\n362\t\n363\tPhone-to-phone at 15 cm is fundamentally constrained by camera pixels per module. From S3,\n364\twe know that below 2.0 camera px/module, erasure is 100%. At 2.25 px/module, we measured\n365\t78% erasure. Objective\n33\t\n34\t> **A static website that accepts a file from the user and turns it into a visual\n35\t> transmission on screen, which a second device running the same page receives through\n36\t> its camera and reconstructs into the original file.**\n37\t>\n38\t> **It must handle large files — on the order of multiple gigabytes.**\n39\t\n40\t- **Static.** No backend. Files on a CDN, works offline, auditable once and trusted\n41\t  thereafter. There is nowhere to upload anything *to*.\n42\t- **Same page, both roles.** One deployment; the user picks sender or receiver.\n43\t- **Screen → camera is the only channel.** Strictly one-way, lossy, low-bandwidth.\n44\t- **Multi-gigabyte.** The requirement that most shapes the architecture (§3).\n45\t\n46\t### 1.1 The honest framing of \"multiple gigabytes\"\n47\t\n48\tMulti-GB support is an **architectural** requirement, not a performance promise. The\n49\tdesign must never *forbid* a large file, run out of memory, or blow up super-linearly.\n50\tBut the channel's physics are what they are:\n51\t\n52\t| File size | Stage 1 (30 KB/s) | Stage 2 (60 KB/s) | Stage 3 (106 KB/s) |\n53\t|---|---|---|---|\n54\t| 100 MB | 57 min | 28 min | 16 min |\n55\t| **1 GB** | **9.7 h** | **4.9 h** | **2.7 h** |\n56\t| **10 GB** | **4.0 days** | **2.0 days** | **27.5 h** |\n57\t| 100 GB | 40.5 days | 20.2 days | 11.4 days |\n58\t| 1 TB | 414 days | 207 days | 117 days |\n59\t\n60\t> All figures are **user-visible file bytes**, not wire bytes. See §13.2 — with\n61\t> compression on, the two differ by 3–10× on compressible input, and quoting the wrong\n62\t> one would overstate throughput.\n63\t\n64\t**Gigabytes are hours-to-days. Terabytes are months.** Three design consequences follow,\n65\tand they are as load-bearing as any coding decision:\n66\t\n67\t1. **Resume is not optional** (D22). Nobody holds a phone for 27 hours.\n68\t2. **Neither side may hold the file in memory** (D20).\n69\t3. **The app states the estimated time before the user commits** (D23). Letting someone\n70\t   start a 40-day transfer without saying so is a product failure, not an edge case.\n71\t\n72\t---\n73\t\n74\t## 2. Glossary\n75\t\n76\tSeveral of these words are overloaded in the surrounding literature, and two of them\n77\t(*block*, *frame*) mean different things in different research documents. Within this\n78\tplan they mean exactly this:\n79\t\n80\t| Term | Meaning here |\n81\t|---|---|\n82\t| **Fragment** | The atomic unit the fountain code operates over. Fixed length **L** for the whole session (D15). |\n83\t| **K** | Number of fragments in one block. Derived as `blockSize / L`; never transmitted (D7). |\n84\t| **Block** | A contiguous slice of the (possibly compressed) payload, cut into K fragments and fountain-coded independently. **Always means this** — never \"fountain block\" or \"QR block\". |\n85\t| **Packet** | One fountain-coded symbol: 13-byte header + L payload bytes. The unit a tile carries. |\n86\t| **Tile** | One QR symbol on screen. Carries exactly one packet. |\n87\t| **Frame** | One displayed image, containing a grid of tiles. **Never** a video frame — those are *camera frames*. |\n88\t| **Camera frame** | One image captured by the receiver's camera. |\n89\t| **Beacon** | A special **packet** carrying file-level metadata instead of payload. Beacon packets are encoded into tiles and mixed into display frames by the frame mixer (D17, §7.2). |\n90\t| **Profile** | A modulation configuration: QR version, module pixel size, tile count. Several coexist per frame (D16). |\n91\t| **Dwell** | How many packets the sender emits for one block before advancing (§8.1). |\n92\t| **Screen px** | A pixel on the *sender's display*. What the renderer controls. |\n93\t| **Camera px** | A pixel in the *receiver's captured frame*. What the decoder actually sees. |\n94\t| **px/module** | **Always CAMERA px per module unless explicitly written \"screen px/module\".** The 4 px/module decode cliff is a *camera*-pixel figure. Conflating the two put every S2/S3 optical run below the cliff — see `../notes/spike-results.md` §S3. |\n95\t| **Magnification** | `camera_px_per_module = screen_px_per_module × M`, where `M` = (capture width across the code region) / (code region width in screen px). A 1920-px-wide landscape code region filling a 1080-px-wide portrait capture gives **M = 0.5625**, so 4 screen px/module is only **2.25 camera px/module**. |\n96\t| **Erasure** | A packet that did not arrive or failed validation. Never a corrupted packet — those are discarded, not used. |\n97\t| **Stage** | A modulation generation: 1 = tiled mono QR, 2 = + RGB tripling, 3 = custom grid codec. |\n98\t| **Pass** | One complete traversal of every block by the sender. |\n99\t\n100\t---"}]},"parent_tool_use_id":"call_cb8a7c63a20941f5b1c300e3","session_id":"b305974a-0f1a-4d77-862e-45c5cfa32b71","uuid":"b814dcba-f43e-4684-9f16-7f2cc10161cc","timestamp":"2026-08-02T23:22:47.059Z","subagent_type":"Explore","task_description":"Explore measurement and §13.2 context"}

It measures the local device's Gaussian Elimination decoder throughput, derives a maximum supported K (`K_max`), and refuses incoming streams whose K parameter exceeds this locally-measured limit.\n10\t\n11\t**Security requirement (T1):** The receiver MUST bounds-check every beacon field before use, including `K ≤ locally benchmarked max (D26)`. Per D26:\n16\t\n17\t> \"K is chosen by the SENDER at session start and MUST be conservative... The receiver derives K from the beacon and MUST refuse a stream whose K exceeds what it benchmarked locally.\"\n18\t\n19\tWithout this component:\n20\t- A sender could transmit K=768 to a low-end device that can only sustain K=512\n21\t- The receiver's GE decoder would fall behind, causing frame drops and transfer failure\n22\t- This creates a resource exhaustion attack vector (T1)\n23\t\n24\t## Component Design\n25\t\n26\t### 1. Benchmark Algorithm\n27\t\n28\tPort the existing `spike/ge-bench.mjs` algorithm to run in browser context:\n29\t\n30\t```typescript\n31\t// src/platform/ge-benchmark.ts\n32\texport interface GEBenchmarkResult {\n33\t  deviceSignature: string;       // UA + platform fingerprint\n34\t  measuredThroughputMBs: number;  // MB/s sustained XOR\n35\t  derivedKMax: number;           // Max K this device can handle\n36\t  timestamp: number;             // When benchmark was run\n37\t}\n38\t\n39\texport interface GEBenchmarkConfig {\n40\t  stages: Array<{name: string, rateKBs: number}>;  // Wire rates to test\n41\t  phoneFactor: number;                               // Safety margin (÷4 default)\n42\t  targetK: number;                                   // K to test (768 default)\n43\t}\n44\t```\n45\t\n46\t**Benchmark procedure:**\n47\t1. Run complete GF(2) GE decode for K=768, L=256\n48\t2. Measure sustained XOR throughput (MB/s)\n49\t3. Apply safety margin (÷4 for desktop→phone estimate)\n50\t4. Derive K_max from the required throughput formula\n51\t\n52\t**Required throughput formula (from §3.1):**\n53\t```\n54\trequired(K, L, wireRate) = K · (K/8 + L) · wireRate / L\n55\t```\n56\t\n57\t**Derive K_max:**\n58\t- Binary search or table lookup to find max K where:\n59\t  `measured_throughput ≥ required(K, 256, stage3_rate)`\n60\t\n61\t### 2. Caching Strategy\n62\t\n63\tCache results in IndexedDB with a composite key:\n64\t\n65\t```typescript\n66\tinterface CacheKey {\n67\t  userAgent: string;          // Navigator UA\n68\t  platform: string;           // 'Win32', 'Linux x86_64', etc.\n69\t  hardwareConcurrency: number; // CPU core count\n70\t  deviceMemory: number;       // GB if available\n71\t}\n72\t\n73\tinterface CachedResult {\n74\t  key: CacheKey;\n75\t  result: GEBenchmarkResult;\n76\t  version: number;            // Benchmark algo version (for invalidation)\n77\t}\n78\t```\n79\t\n80\t**Cache invalidation:**\n81\t- Version bump when benchmark algorithm changes\n82\t- Optional: time-based expiry (30 days)\n83\t- Manual: user-triggered \"re-benchmark\" in health check UI\n84\t\n85\t### 3. Integration with Health Check (§16.4)\n86\t\n87\tThe health check runs before the user commits to receiving a file. Current checklist (§16.4):\n88\t- Storage estimate (bf-4d6)\n89\t- Camera capability and measured fps (D14)\n90\t- Wake lock availability\n91\t- OPFS write test\n92\t- Calibration probe (D11)\n93\t\n94\t**Add:** GE benchmark (this component)\n95\t\n96\t```typescript\n97\t// src/platform/health-check.ts\n98\texport interface HealthCheckResult {\n99\t  storage: {available: boolean, quota?: number};\n100\t  camera: {available: boolean, measuredFps?: number};\n101\t  wakeLock: {available: boolean};\n102\t  opfs: {available: boolean, writeTestPassed?: boolean};\n103\t  geBenchmark: {available: boolean, kMax?: number};  // NEW\n104\t  calibration: {lumaWins: boolean | null};  // D11\n105\t}\n106\t\n107\texport async function runHealthCheck(): Promise<HealthCheckResult> {\n108\t  return {\n109\t    storage: await checkStorage(),\n110\t    camera: await checkCamera(),\n111\t    wakeLock: await checkWakeLock(),\n112\t    opfs: await checkOPFS(),\n113\t    geBenchmark: await runGEBenchmark(),  // NEW\n114\t    calibration: await runCalibrationProbe(),\n115\t  };\n116\t}\n117\t```\n118\t\n119\t### 4. Stream Validation (D26/T1 Enforcement)\n120\t\n121\tOn beacon receipt, before allocating any GE structures:\n122\t\n123\t```typescript\n124\t// src/core/frame/beacon.ts (or validation layer)\n125\texport function validateBeacon(meta: BeaconMeta, localKMax: number): void {\n126\t  // ... existing bounds checks (originalSize, payloadLen, blockCount, L, etc.)\n127\t  \n128\t  // NEW: D26 K validation\n129\t  const derivedK = Math.ceil(meta.blockSize / L);\n130\t  if (derivedK > localKMax) {\n131\t    throw new StreamRefusedError(\n132\t      'E-K-OVERFLOW',\n133\t      `Sender K (${derivedK}) exceeds this device's maximum (${localKMax}). ` +\n134\t      `Reduce file size or use a more powerful receiver.`,\n135\t      {derivedK, localKMax}\n136\t    );\n137\t  }\n138\t}\n139\t```\n140\t\n141\t### 5. Error Code\n142\t\n143\t**Error code:** `E-K-OVERFLOW` (new addition to §11 error taxonomy)\n144\t\n145\t| Field | Value |\n146\t|-------|-------|\n147\t| Code | `E-K-OVERFLOW` |\n148\t| Category | Protocol |\n149\t| Meaning | Beacon-derived K exceeds local device's benchmarked K_max |\n150\t| User-facing | \"That transmission is too complex for this device. Use a smaller file or a more powerful receiver.\" |\n151\t| Recovery | User must act on the OTHER device (reduce file size → smaller K), or use a desktop as receiver |\n152\t\n153\t**Why not `E-META-BOUNDS`**: T1 groups this under meta bounds, but K_overflow is a distinct condition with different recovery (it's about computational capacity, not malformed data). Keeping it separate makes debugging and telemetry clearer.\n154\t\n155\t### 6. Worker Architecture\n156\t\n157\tRun the benchmark in a dedicated worker to avoid janking the UI:\n158\t\n159\t```typescript\n160\t// src/workers/ge-benchmark.worker.ts\n161\texport interface BenchmarkMessage {\n162\t  type: 'run';\n163\t  config: GEBenchmarkConfig;\n164\t}\n165\t\n166\texport interface BenchmarkResultMessage {\n167\t  type: 'result';\n168\t  result: GEBenchmarkResult;\n169\t}\n170\t\n171\t// Worker spins up, runs the GE decode loop (ported from spike/ge-bench.mjs),\n172\t// measures throughput, posts back result, self-terminates.\n173\t```\n174\t\n175\t**Main thread:**\n176\t1. Fallback and Graceful Degradation\n183\t\n184\tIf the benchmark fails to run (e.g., worker crash, timeout):\n185\t\n186\t```typescript\n187\texport const FALLBACK_K_MAX = 512;  // Conservative default\n188\t\n189\texport async function getKMaxWithFallback(): Promise<number> {\n190\t  try {\n191\t    const cached = await loadCachedBenchmark();\n192\t    if (cached) return cached.derivedKMax;\n193\t    \n194\t    const fresh = await runGEBenchmark();\n195\t    await cacheBenchmark(fresh);\n196\t    return fresh.derivedKMax;\n197\t  } catch (e) {\n198\t    console.warn('GE benchmark failed, using fallback K_max=512', e);\n199\t    return FALLBACK_K_MAX;\n200\t  }\n201\t}\n202\t```\n203\t\n204\t**Rationale for K=512 fallback:**\n205\t- Stage 3 required: 69.5 MB/s at K=512 (from §3.1 table)\n206\t- After ÷4 phone factor: desktop needs 278 MB/s\n207\t- S1 measured 3,260 MB/s on desktop → 11.7× margin\n208\t- Even if phone is 8× slower (not 4×), 512 works\n209\t\n210\t### 8. These scripts orchestrate real-world device testing where one device sends and another receives via camera.\n\n## Files\n\n### `devrig.sh` — Two-device rig orchestration\n\nDrives the two-device optical rig for Phase 0.5 S2/S3/S4 measurements with no human in the loop (except for physically aiming the phone at the bench screen).\n\n**Setup:**\n- **bench (Lenovo T450s, X on :0, 1920×1080)** → SENDER, Chromium kiosk mode\n- **Pixel 6 over ADB** → RECEIVER, Chrome\n- **this host** → Vite HTTPS server + orchestration\n\n**HTTPS is mandatory:** `getUserMedia` needs a secure context, so the phone must load the receiver over a real certificate. The script uses `tailscale cert` to issue one for this host's tailnet name, which means no interstitial to tap through — important when driving via ADB.\n\n**Usage:**\n```bash\ntools/devrig.sh serve      # Start the dev server (foreground)\ntools/devrig.sh cert       # (re)issue the TLS cert\ntools/devrig.sh send R2 4 4 3 12\ntools/devrig.sh recv R2 4 4 3 12\ntools/devrig.sh run  R2 4 4 3 12 45     # Both ends, wait N seconds, collect results\ntools/devrig.sh shots                   # Screenshot both screens\ntools/devrig.sh stop\n```\n\n**Parameters:** `rung mod cols rows fps` (e.g., `R2 4 4 3 12`)\n- `rung`: Modulation profile (R1=conservative v10-L, R2=nominal v15-L, R3=aggressive v20-L)\n- `mod`: Module size (screen pixels)\n- `cols`, `rows`: Grid dimensions\n- `fps`: Frame rate\n\n**Outputs:**\n- Screenshots saved to `test-results/`\n- `window.sfStats` scraped via Chrome DevTools Protocol and saved as JSON\n\n### `cdp_eval.py` — Chrome DevTools Protocol evaluator\n\nEvaluates JavaScript expressions in a Chrome tab over the DevTools protocol.\n\n**Used by `devrig.sh`** to read `window.sfStats` off the phone without OCR — the numbers matter too much to read them out of a JPEG.\n\n**Usage:**\n```bash\npython3 cdp_eval.py <ws-url> '<js expression>'\n```\n\n**Protocol:** Speaks just enough WebSocket framing to avoid dependencies — payloads are small and single-frame.\n\n## Onboarding Constraints — HTTPS via Tailscale cert\n\nThe rig requires HTTPS for camera access (`getUserMedia` needs a secure context). This is documented in `vite.config.ts` but **absent from plan.md §16.2**:\n\n1. **Certificate issuance:** Run `sudo tailscale cert --cert-file .certs/sf.crt --key-file .certs/sf.key <host>.<tailnet>.ts.net`\n2. **Vite configuration:** `vite.config.ts` loads these certificates for the dev server\n3. **No interstitial:** The Tailscale-issued cert is trusted by the phone, avoiding manual certificate acceptance that would block ADB-driven testing\n\n**This is a real onboarding constraint:** Developers setting up the rig for the first time must:\n- Have Tailscale installed\n- Be on the same tailnet\n- Run the certificate issuance step before starting the server\n- Keep certificates refreshed (Tailscale certs expire)\n\n## Relationship to Testing Tiers\n\nThis rig enables **T-physical-rig** (plan.md §14.1), which is:\n- **Two real devices, fixed mounting, the §13.2 denominator**\n- **The acceptance gate for §13.1 throughput** — nothing else can measure it\n- Runs **per release**\n\nThe rig measures the actual optical channel performance under controlled conditions, which is the only way to validate the throughput budgets in §13.1.\n\n## Relationship to Spike\n\nUnlike `spike/` (which is deleted once results land per spike/README.md), this directory is **retained infrastructure** because:\n- The optical rig is needed for **every release** (T-physical-rig runs per release)\n- S2/S3/S4 measurements may need to be repeated as the system evolves\n- The scripts are reusable instrumentation, not one-time experiments\n- They provide the canonical way to measure §13.1's optical budgets\n\nThe rig itself is not the spike — the spike is the throwaway code that generates test patterns.
